Stochastic Matching with Polynomial Degree

Soheil Behnezhad ††thanks: Supported in part by NSF CAREER Award CCF 2442812, a Sloan Fellowship, and a Google Research Award. Affiliation: Northeastern University
Abstract

We study the stochastic matching problem, where a graph GG is known in advance, but each edge survives independently with probability pp. The goal is to select a subgraph HH of small maximum degree before seeing the surviving edges, while preserving a (1−ε)(1-\varepsilon) fraction of the expected maximum matching size. This problem has received significant attention due to its numerous applications in kidney exchange, labor markets, and online dating.

In this paper, we show there is always a subgraph H⊆GH\subseteq G achieving a (1−ε)(1-\varepsilon)-approximation while having a maximum degree of at most

O⁡(log⁡(1/ε)ε4⋅1p).O\left(\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{\varepsilon^{4}}\cdot\frac{1}{p}\right).

This resolves a major conjecture of the literature, first stated by [ BDH, STOC’20], that poly⁡(1ε​p)\mathrm{poly}(\frac{1}{\varepsilon p}) degrees suffice. The best previous bound was (1/p)exp⁡((1/ε)​log⁡(1/ε))(1/p)^{\exp((1/\varepsilon)\log(1/\varepsilon))} by [ ABGR, STOC’25].

The key to this result is a lemma of independent interest that any distribution over the matchings of a stochastic graph can be transformed to another distribution which matches each vertex with exactly the same probability, but exhibits extremely low total pairwise correlation.

1 Introduction

The stochastic matching problem, introduced by Blum et al. [Blum15], is a model for finding large matchings when edge availability is uncertain and must be learned through expensive queries. The problem is motivated by applications in kidney exchange, online labor markets, and online dating. These applications, together with the rich mathematical structure underlying its simple formulation, have led to a flurry of results over the last decade [Blum15, AKL16, AKL17, BR18, AB19, BFHR19, BDFHR19, GKS19, BDH20, BD20, BBD22, FGH22, ABGR25, DS25].

Formally, let G=(V,E)G=(V,E) be a known graph and let GpG_{p} be an (unknown) random subgraph of GG retaining every edge independently with probability p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1]. An algorithm selects a subgraph H⊆GH\subseteq G, queries its edges, and returns a maximum matching in H∩GpH\cap G_{p}. Writing μ\mu for maximum matching size, the goal is to choose HH (without knowing the realization GpG_{p}) such that

E⁡μ⁡(H∩Gp)≥(1−ε)​E⁡μ⁡(Gp).\E\mu(H\cap G_{p})\geq(1-\varepsilon)\E\mu(G_{p}). (1)

While simply taking H=GH=G (i.e., querying all edges) clearly satisfies 1, the goal is to keep the maximum degree Δ⁡(H)\Delta(H) of HH, which corresponds to the number of queries per vertex, small.

Previous results.

The earlier works [Blum15, AKL16, AKL17, BFHR19, AB19] focused on improving the approximation, initially from close to 1/2 and later to 2/3, while keeping the maximum degree dependent only on pp. The first work to show a (1−ε)(1-\varepsilon)-approximation is achievable with degree Oε,p​(1)O_{\varepsilon,p}(1) was that of Behnezhad, Derakhshan, and Hajiaghayi [BDH20] who achieved so by

Δ⁡(H)≤(1/p)(log⁡(1/p))exp⁡(O⁡(1/ε)).\Delta(H)\leq(1/p)^{(\log(1/p))^{\exp(O(1/\varepsilon))}}.

They further conjectured that the same algorithm should achieve Δ⁡(H)≤poly⁡(1/(ε​p))\Delta(H)\leq\mathrm{poly}(1/(\varepsilon p)) which has remained a major open problem since. Partial progress was made by [ABGR25] who obtained

Δ⁡(H)≤(1/p)exp⁡((1/ε)​log⁡(1/ε)),\Delta(H)\leq(1/p)^{\exp((1/\varepsilon)\log(1/\varepsilon))},

which is poly⁡(1/p)\mathrm{poly}(1/p) for fixed ε\varepsilon, but far from poly⁡(1/(ε​p))\mathrm{poly}(1/(\varepsilon p)).

Main result.

In this paper, we prove that the conjecture of [BDH20] is true.

A few remarks:

  • •

    To prove Result 1, we analyze the sample-and-union algorithm of [BFHR19] (formalized as Algorithm 1) which is also the algorithm analyzed and conjectured to work by [BDH20].

  • •

    In Appendix A we present a lower bound of Ω⁡(ε−1​p−1)\Omega(\varepsilon^{-1}p^{-1}), which shows that the pp-dependency of Result 1 is optimal.

  • •

    The upper bound of Result 1 could be further improved to O⁡(ε−2​p−1+ε−3)O\left(\varepsilon^{-2}p^{-1}+\varepsilon^{-3}\right) using a slightly different algorithm and a more intricate analysis (still based on Lemma 3.1). The main body of this paper presents the slightly weaker bound of Result 1 for readability and clarity of presentation. We discuss the needed modifications for the improvement in Appendix B.

2 Technical Overview

Crucial and noncrucial edges.

We begin by recalling the crucial/noncrucial edge decomposition introduced by Behnezhad, Farhadi, Hajiaghayi, and Reyhani [BFHR19], which has since become a central ingredient in the analysis of stochastic matching algorithms. Fix a deterministic maximum matching algorithm 𝖬𝖬⁡(⋅)\MM(\cdot), and for every edge ee, let

qe:=Pr[e∈𝖬𝖬(Gp)]q_{e}:=\Pr[e\in\MM(G_{p})]

denote its probability of belonging to the selected maximum matching of a random realization. For a threshold τ>0\tau>0, an edge is called crucial if qe≥τq_{e}\geq\tau, and noncrucial otherwise.

Crucial edges are easy to preserve: since ∑e∋vqe≤1\sum_{e\ni v}q_{e}\leq 1, every vertex has at most 1/τ1/\tau crucial edges, so we can afford to include all of them in HH. On the other hand, there may be arbitrarily many noncrucial edges, but the hope is that they can be used interchangeably: since each is rarely used by the optimum, preserving sufficiently many alternatives should suffice.

The challenge is that both types of edges can contribute substantially to the optimum, and we must preserve their contributions simultaneously. A simple example is a large clique with a private leaf attached to each vertex, as illustrated on the right. When p=1/2p=1/2, roughly half the clique vertices can be matched to their leaves, while the remaining vertices can be matched inside. Thus, both types of edges contribute substantially, even though each individual clique edge has a very small selection probability.

The independence approach.

A key insight of Behnezhad, Derakhshan, and Hajiaghayi [BDH20] was that we can first commit to a matching MCM_{C} of realized crucial edges, and only then reveal the realization of the noncrucial edges, provided that the crucial matching is chosen with sufficient independence.

To see why independence matters, consider a noncrucial edge e=(u,v)e=(u,v), and suppose that each of its endpoints is matched by MCM_{C} with probability 1/21/2. For us to be able to use ee, both endpoints must remain unmatched by MCM_{C}. If their matching events were independent, this would happen with probability 1/41/4. However, these events could be perfectly negatively correlated: for example, exactly one of uu and vv might always be matched by MCM_{C}. In this case, both vertices are individually unmatched with probability 1/21/2, yet the probability that they are simultaneously unmatched is zero, meaning that we can never use the edge ee.

Unfortunately, full independence is impossible: whenever a vertex is matched, at least one of its neighbors must also be matched. The approach of [BDH20] was therefore to construct a crucial matching in which sufficiently distant vertices are matched independently. They accomplished this using a distributed LOCAL algorithm whose output at a vertex depends only on randomness within a neighborhood of radius Oε​(log⁡ΔC)O_{\varepsilon}(\log\Delta_{C}), where ΔC\Delta_{C} denotes the maximum degree of the crucial graph. Consequently, the matching status of a vertex can be dependent on that of as many as ΔCOε​(log⁡ΔC)\Delta_{C}^{O_{\varepsilon}(\log\Delta_{C})} other vertices. This quasipolynomial dependence on ΔC\Delta_{C} is ultimately responsible for the quasipolynomial dependence on 1/p1/p in their result.

The subsequent work of Azarmehr, Behnezhad, Ghafari, and Rubinfeld [ABGR25] substantially improved this approach using local computation algorithms (LCAs). By carefully bounding both the in-queries and out-queries, they obtained an expected correlated-set size of only ΔCpoly⁡(1/ε).\Delta_{C}^{\mathrm{poly}(1/\varepsilon)}. This improvement was sufficient to obtain a degree bound polynomial in 1/p1/p for every fixed ε\varepsilon. Nevertheless, the exponent of this polynomial still depends on ε\varepsilon.

Our key lemma: bounding total covariance.

We take a different approach. Rather than requiring a vertex to be independent of almost every other vertex, we bound the total strength of the correlations between all pairs of vertices.

Our key lemma shows that every matching distribution can be transformed into another matching distribution that preserves the probability of matching each vertex exactly, while having extremely small total covariance.

In particular, the total covariance is bounded by a constant times the expected number of matched vertices, with no dependence on the maximum degree of the graph. This does not mean that each vertex is correlated with only constantly many others: a vertex may be weakly correlated with many vertices, but the sum of the magnitudes of these correlations is small.

An illustrative example.

What makes the lemma particularly surprising is that it preserves every vertex’s matching probability exactly. In fact, there are examples where these marginals uniquely determine the matching algorithm. To appreciate the strength of this statement, consider a path PnP_{n} on vertices v1,…,vnv_{1},\ldots,v_{n}, where every edge survives independently with probability pp. Let MM be the greedy algorithm that processes edges from left to right, selecting each surviving edge if the left endpoint is unmatched.

It could be confirmed that the greedy left-to-right algorithm is the only algorithm that achieves these exact marginals. For example, (v1,v2)(v_{1},v_{2}) must be in the matching whenever realized to ensure v1v_{1} gets matched with probability pp. And (v2,v3)(v_{2},v_{3}) must be in the matching whenever (v2,v3)(v_{2},v_{3}) is realized and (v1,v2)(v_{1},v_{2}) is not to make sure the marginal contribution of v2v_{2} is satisfied. This means that to preserve the marginals, the proof of Lemma 3.1 cannot modify this matching MM at all (at least in this example). Instead, we have to show that the total covariance remains remarkable small, despite the apparent propagation of dependencies along this long path.

Proof idea for the key lemma.

The proof is based on a surprisingly simple optimization rule: assign each vertex a randomly perturbed weight

wv=θv+ξv,w_{v}=\theta_{v}+\xi_{v},

where θv\theta_{v} is a deterministic offset and the perturbation ξv∼𝖴𝗇𝗂𝖿⁡[−1,1]\xi_{v}\sim\mathsf{Unif}[-1,1] is chosen independently for each vertex. We then choose a matching maximizing the total weight of its covered vertices.

There are two main ingredients in the analysis.

First, we show that the offsets can be chosen to preserve the prescribed vertex marginals. This is far from obvious a priori. Why should maximizing a linear function of randomly perturbed vertex weights be capable of reproducing an arbitrary feasible vector of vertex-matching probabilities? We prove this using a potential-function argument. If a vertex is matched less frequently than desired, we increase its offset; if it is matched too frequently, we decrease it. The challenge is that changing the weight of a vertex could drastically affect the marginals on other vertices. Nonetheless, we show that these updates make progress toward the target marginals by decreasing a suitable potential function. This produces matching distributions whose marginals can be made arbitrarily close to the desired ones. Finally, by taking a limit of these distributions, rather than a limit of the offsets themselves, we obtain the target marginals exactly.

Second, we exploit the stability of the vertex-weighted matching objective. The key observation is that changing the weight of a single vertex, together with any subset of its incident edges, changes the optimal covered set at at most two vertices. This stability property is particularly powerful because all the randomness can be grouped into independent blocks, one for each vertex. Resampling any single block then changes the coverage-indicator vector in at most two coordinates. We analyze the resulting vector of coverage indicators using a martingale. The small effect of resampling one block translates into a bound on the martingale differences, which in turn bounds the total pairwise covariance.

3 Key lemma: bounding total covariance

In this section, we prove the key lemma used in the paper.

We note that while the lemma preserves vertex marginals, it may not necessarily match edges with the same probability. We write sv:=E⁡[Xv]s_{v}:=\E[X_{v}] to the target matching probability of vv.

Proof outline.

To prove Lemma 3.1, we assign a carefully randomized (and possibly negative) weight to each vertex and let ℬ\mathcal{B} be the matching that maximizes the total weight of covered vertices. In Section 3.2 prove that maximizing the vertex weights has the desired bound on the total pairwise covariance of all vertices. The harder part of the proof is to show there exists an assignment of weights such that the marginals are satisfied; we prove this in Section 3.3 using a combinatorial potential-based argument.

3.1 Stability of vertex weighted matchings

First, we show that the matching that maximizes vertex weights is stable. This observation and its proof are rather standard in the literature of matching. We present the proof anyway for completeness.

We say a weight vector w∈ℝVw\in\mathbb{R}^{V} is generic if distinct vertex subsets have distinct weight sums. Note that for generic ww, every matching LL maximizing ∑v∈V⁡(L)wv\sum_{v\in V(L)}w_{v} has the same covered set. We denote this set by S⁡(G,w)S(G,w). The optimization is over all matchings, including the empty matching; it has no additional cardinality constraint. Weights may be negative.

Lemma 3.2 (Stability of the optimal covered set).

Let ww be generic. Deleting a vertex ii from GG either leaves the optimal covered set unchanged or changes it by the symmetric difference {i,j}\{i,j\} for some j≠ij\neq i. A change is possible only if ii is covered in S⁡(G,w)S(G,w).

More generally, suppose (G,w)(G,w) and (G′,w′)(G^{\prime},w^{\prime}) differ only in edges incident to ii and in the weight of ii, and both weight vectors are generic. Then

|S⁡(G,w)△S⁡(G′,w′)|≤2.|S(G,w)\mathbin{\triangle}S(G^{\prime},w^{\prime})|\leq 2.

If the sets differ, at least one of them contains ii.

Proof.

Let LL be an optimal matching in GG and L−L^{-} an optimal matching in G−iG-i. Regard both as matchings on V⁡(G)V(G), with ii isolated in the second instance. Their symmetric difference has maximum degree two, and thus decomposes into alternating paths and even cycles.

Consider a component not containing ii. Switching the edges of this component in LL is feasible in GG, and switching it in L−L^{-} is feasible in G−iG-i. If the difference between the two covered-weight sums on this component is dd, the two optimality inequalities give d≥0d\geq 0 and d≤0d\leq 0. Thus d=0d=0. Genericity implies that the two covered sets on this component agree.

If a component contains ii, it is a path with endpoint ii: the matching L−L^{-} has no edge at ii. Every internal vertex is covered by both matchings, and only the two endpoints can change coverage. Thus the covered sets either agree or differ exactly at ii and the other endpoint. If ii is uncovered by LL, there is no such component, and the sets agree everywhere.

For the second part, delete ii from both instances. This leaves the same graph and the same generic weights. Let TT be its unique optimal covered set. Each original covered set is either TT or T△{i,j}T\mathbin{\triangle}\{i,j\} for some j≠ij\neq i. Any two sets of these forms differ at at most two vertices. If neither original set contains ii, both equal TT. ∎

3.3 Satisfying vertex marginals by weight updates

In this section, we show that we could set the deterministic offsets θ∈ℝV\theta\in\mathbb{R}^{V} such that the resulting random matching MθM^{\theta} of G⁡(ω)G(\omega) that maximizes the covered vertex weights wv=θv+ξvw_{v}=\theta_{v}+\xi_{v} for independent perturbations ξv∼𝖴𝗇𝗂𝖿⁡[−1,1]\xi_{v}\sim\mathsf{Unif}[-1,1] satisfies the marginals of the matching 𝒜⁡(G⁡(ω))\mathcal{A}(G(\omega)). Namely, let XX be the coverage vector of M=𝒜⁡(G⁡(ω))M=\mathcal{A}(G(\omega)) with target marginals sv=E⁡Xvs_{v}=\E X_{v}, and let XθX^{\theta} be the coverage vector of MθM^{\theta} with vertex marginals mv​(θ):=E⁡Xvθm_{v}(\theta):=\E X_{v}^{\theta}. We prove in this section that there exists θ\theta such that mv​(θ)=svm_{v}(\theta)=s_{v} for all vv.

We do so by iteratively updating the offsets. The update has a simple interpretation. If mv​(θ)<svm_{v}(\theta)<s_{v}, increase the reward for covering vv; if mv​(θ)>svm_{v}(\theta)>s_{v}, decrease it. The challenge is that changing this reward can also change other vertices’ coverage probabilities. To analyze this, we define a potential function.

Lemma 3.3 (Calibration by single-vertex updates).

Let ρ∈(0,1)\rho\in(0,1). Start with θ=0\theta=0. Whenever |sv−mv​(θ)|>ρ|s_{v}-m_{v}(\theta)|>\rho for some vertex vv, make the update

h:=sv−mv​(θ),θv←θv+h,h:=s_{v}-m_{v}(\theta),\qquad\theta_{v}\leftarrow\theta_{v}+h, (8)

leaving all other offsets unchanged. Fix a deterministic rule for choosing a violating vertex. After at most ⌈2​n/ρ2⌉\lceil 2n/\rho^{2}\rceil updates, the process stops at a deterministic vector θ(ρ)\theta^{(\rho)} satisfying

maxv⁡|mv​(θ(ρ))−sv|≤ρ,‖θ(ρ)‖∞≤2​nρ.\max_{v}|m_{v}(\theta^{(\rho)})-s_{v}|\leq\rho,\qquad\|\theta^{(\rho)}\|_{\infty}\leq\frac{2n}{\rho}. (9)
Proof.

We analyze a change to one coordinate while keeping all other offsets fixed, and then bound the total number of changes.

The potential.

For a feasible matching LL and fixed perturbations, define its score by

Wθ​(L):=∑u∈V⁡(L)(θu+ξu).W_{\theta}(L):=\sum_{u\in V(L)}(\theta_{u}+\xi_{u}).

Define the expected optimal score and the potential by

F⁡(θ):=E⁡Wθ​(Mθ),Ψ⁡(θ):=F⁡(θ)−∑uθu​su.F(\theta):=\E W_{\theta}(M^{\theta}),\qquad\Psi(\theta):=F(\theta)-\sum_{u}\theta_{u}s_{u}. (10)

On every realized graph, MM is a feasible competitor for MθM^{\theta}. Since ξ\xi has mean zero and is independent of XX,

E⁡Wθ​(M)=∑uθu​su,Ψ⁡(θ)=E⁡[Wθ​(Mθ)−Wθ​(M)]≥0.\E W_{\theta}(M)=\sum_{u}\theta_{u}s_{u},\qquad\Psi(\theta)=\E\bigl[W_{\theta}(M^{\theta})-W_{\theta}(M)\bigr]\geq 0.

Also

0≤Ψ⁡(0)=F⁡(0)≤n,0\leq\Psi(0)=F(0)\leq n, (11)

because at zero offsets every covered vertex contributes at most one.

How one vertex’s coverage probability responds.

Let θ′\theta^{\prime} agree with θ\theta except that θv′=θv+h\theta^{\prime}_{v}=\theta_{v}+h, where hh is any real number. Condition on the realized graph and on all perturbations except ξv\xi_{v}. If some matching covers vv, define

A:=maxL:v∈V⁡(L)∑u∈V⁡(L)∖{v}(θu+ξu),B:=maxL:v∉V⁡(L)∑u∈V⁡(L)(θu+ξu),\displaystyle A:=\max_{L:\,v\in V(L)}\sum_{u\in V(L)\setminus\{v\}}(\theta_{u}+\xi_{u}),\qquad\qquad B:=\max_{L:\,v\notin V(L)}\sum_{u\in V(L)}(\theta_{u}+\xi_{u}),

where both maxima range over matchings in this fixed realized graph. The empty matching makes the second class nonempty. Every matching in the first class receives the same contribution θv+ξv\theta_{v}+\xi_{v} from vv; the definition of AA removes that contribution. Thus neither AA nor BB depends on θv\theta_{v} or ξv\xi_{v}, and both remain unchanged when θv\theta_{v} is updated.

The best score in the first class is θv+ξv+A\theta_{v}+\xi_{v}+A; the best score in the second is BB. Therefore, except on a probability-zero tie, the optimal matching covers vv exactly when

ξv>B−A−θv.\xi_{v}>B-A-\theta_{v}.

The update changes this threshold by −h-h. Since ξv\xi_{v} is uniform on an interval of length two, the conditional coverage probability changes by at most |h|/2|h|/2. If no matching covers vv, that probability is zero under both offsets. Averaging over the conditioning gives

|mv​(θ′)−mv​(θ)|≤|h|2.|m_{v}(\theta^{\prime})-m_{v}(\theta)|\leq\frac{|h|}{2}. (12)

Comparing the old and new optimal scores.

Use the same realized graph and the same perturbations to choose MθM^{\theta} and Mθ′M^{\theta^{\prime}}. The matching Mθ′M^{\theta^{\prime}} is feasible under the old weights, so optimality of MθM^{\theta} gives Wθ​(Mθ′)≤Wθ​(Mθ)W_{\theta}(M^{\theta^{\prime}})\leq W_{\theta}(M^{\theta}). The score of the fixed matching Mθ′M^{\theta^{\prime}}, according to the new weights θ′\theta^{\prime}, only differs from that of θ\theta by exactly hh iff vv is matched by Mθ′M^{\theta^{\prime}}. Therefore,

Wθ′​(Mθ′)−Wθ​(Mθ′)=h​Xvθ′.W_{\theta^{\prime}}(M^{\theta^{\prime}})-W_{\theta}(M^{\theta^{\prime}})=hX_{v}^{\theta^{\prime}}. (13)

Here Xvθ′X_{v}^{\theta^{\prime}} is one if the particular vertex vv is covered by Mθ′M^{\theta^{\prime}} and zero otherwise. Thus the score difference is hh or zero: only vv’s weight changed. Combining the two score comparisons yields

Wθ′​(Mθ′)−Wθ​(Mθ)\displaystyle W_{\theta^{\prime}}(M^{\theta^{\prime}})-W_{\theta}(M^{\theta}) =[Wθ′​(Mθ′)−Wθ​(Mθ′)]+[Wθ​(Mθ′)−Wθ​(Mθ)]≤h​Xvθ′.\displaystyle=\bigl[W_{\theta^{\prime}}(M^{\theta^{\prime}})-W_{\theta}(M^{\theta^{\prime}})\bigr]+\bigl[W_{\theta}(M^{\theta^{\prime}})-W_{\theta}(M^{\theta})\bigr]\leq hX_{v}^{\theta^{\prime}}.

Taking expectations, and subtracting the change h​svhs_{v} in the target term of the potential, gives

Ψ⁡(θ′)−Ψ⁡(θ)≤h⁡(mv​(θ′)−sv).\Psi(\theta^{\prime})-\Psi(\theta)\leq h\bigl(m_{v}(\theta^{\prime})-s_{v}\bigr). (14)

Note that the inequality holds for either sign of hh.

Every inaccurate coordinate gives a definite decrease.

Choose h=sv−mv​(θ)h=s_{v}-m_{v}(\theta) as in (8). By (14) and (12),

Ψ⁡(θ′)−Ψ⁡(θ)≤h⁡(mv​(θ′)−mv​(θ))−h2≤|h|​|mv​(θ′)−mv​(θ)|−h2≤−h22.\Psi(\theta^{\prime})-\Psi(\theta)\leq h\bigl(m_{v}(\theta^{\prime})-m_{v}(\theta)\bigr)-h^{2}\leq|h|\,|m_{v}(\theta^{\prime})-m_{v}(\theta)|-h^{2}\leq-\frac{h^{2}}{2}.

Thus every performed update decreases the potential by more than ρ2/2\rho^{2}/2. The potential starts at most nn and is always nonnegative by (11), so the process must stop within ⌈2​n/ρ⌉\lceil 2n/\rho\rceil updates. When the process terminates, no coordinate violates the desired accuracy. ∎

Getting exact marginals.

At first, it may seem that applying Lemma 3.3 and letting ρk:=1/k\rho_{k}:=1/k, θ(k):=θ⁡(ρk)\theta^{(k)}:=\theta(\rho_{k}), and taking the limit θ⋆=limk→∞θ(k)\theta^{\star}=\lim_{k\to\infty}\theta^{(k)} would achieve exact marginals. However, note that Lemma 3.3 only gives ‖θ⁡(ρ)‖∞≤2​n/ρ\|\theta(\rho)\|_{\infty}\leq 2n/\rho which diverges as ρ→0\rho\to 0.

The trick is to take the limit of distributions, and not the weights. We apply Lemma 3.3 along any sequence ρk↓0\rho_{k}\downarrow 0. For each kk, use the fixed deterministic offsets θ(ρk)\theta^{(\rho_{k})} on a fresh realized graph with independent perturbations. The random object (G⁡(ω),M(k))(G(\omega),M^{(k)}) is a joint distribution over a finite space since the graph is finite and the set of matchings is also finite. It therefore has a convergent subsequence. Its limit has the original graph-realization distribution, is supported on feasible matchings, and has coverage marginals exactly ss by (9). Define 𝒜′\mathcal{A}^{\prime} to sample from the limiting conditional law of the matching given G⁡(ω)G(\omega), using a private independent seed, and write M′=𝒜′​(G⁡(ω))M^{\prime}=\mathcal{A}^{\prime}(G(\omega)) and X′v=𝟏{v∈V(M′)}X^{\prime}_{v}=\mathbf{1}_{\{v\in V(M^{\prime})\}}. Thus E⁡Xv′=sv=E⁡Xv\E X^{\prime}_{v}=s_{v}=\E X_{v} for every vertex vv.

4 Proof of the main theorem using Lemma 3.1

In this section we prove that the sample-and-union algorithm achieves a (1−ε)(1-\varepsilon)-approximation with degree O⁡(log⁡(1/ε)p​ε4)O(\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{p\varepsilon^{4}}). The proof is more or less an adaptation of the arguments of [BDH20, ABGR25] to the total covariance upper bound of Lemma 3.1.

Theorem 1.

For every graph GG, p∈(0,1]p\in(0,1], and ε∈(0,1)\varepsilon\in(0,1), the output HH of Algorithm 1 achieves a (1−ε)(1-\varepsilon)-approximation with maximum degree R=O⁡(log⁡(1/ε)p​ε4).R=O\!\left(\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{p\varepsilon^{4}}\right).

Remark 4.1.

Algorithm 1, for maximum degree R=O⁡(log⁡(1/ε)​(1p​ε2+1ε3))R=O\left(\log(1/\varepsilon)(\frac{1}{p\varepsilon^{2}}+\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{3}})\right), also could be shown to achieve a (1−ε)(1-\varepsilon)-approximation using a slightly more complicated analysis. The log⁡(1/ε)\log(1/\varepsilon) factor could further be removed from this bound by switching to a different algorithm. See Appendix B.

4.1 Notation and elementary tools

Notation.

All graphs in the main argument are finite, undirected, and simple. All logarithms are natural. Constants hidden in asymptotic notation are absolute. For a matching MM, let V⁡(M)V(M) be its covered vertices. Write μ⁡(K)\mu(K) for the maximum cardinality of a matching in KK and 𝖬𝖬⁡(K)\MM(K) for the matching chosen by the fixed rule. A subscript pp denotes independent edge survival with probability pp. Intersections of graphs refer to their edge sets on the common vertex set.

For a nonnegative edge vector zz, use

|z|:=∑eze,zv:=∑e∋vze,z⁡(F):=∑e∈Fze.|z|:=\sum_{e}z_{e},\qquad z_{v}:=\sum_{e\ni v}z_{e},\qquad z(F):=\sum_{e\in F}z_{e}.

The vector is a fractional matching if zv≤1z_{v}\leq 1 for every vertex. Let EK​(S)E_{K}(S) be the edges of KK with both endpoints in SS. All sums of covariances indexed by u,vu,v are over ordered pairs and include the diagonal.

Tools.

We now mention some elementary tools we use to turn a fractional assignment into an integral matching.

Lemma 4.2 (A positive-part bound).

For b>0b>0 and r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R},

(r−b)+≤r24​b,(r)+:=max⁡{r,0}.(r-b)_{+}\leq\frac{r^{2}}{4b},\qquad(r)_{+}:=\max\{r,0\}.

Consequently, if WW has finite variance and c>E⁡Wc>\E W, then

E⁡(W−c)+≤Var⁡(W)4​(c−E⁡W).\E(W-c)_{+}\leq\frac{\Var(W)}{4(c-\E W)}.
Proof.

The first inequality is immediate for r≤br\leq b. For r>br>b it is equivalent to 0≤(r−2​b)20\leq(r-2b)^{2}. Apply it with r=W−E⁡Wr=W-\E W and b=c−E⁡Wb=c-\E W, and take expectations. ∎

Theorem 2 (Matching polytope; Edmonds [Edmonds65]).

A nonnegative edge vector zz on a finite loopless graph is a convex combination of incidence vectors of matchings if and only if

zv≤1for every ​v,z⁡(EK​(S))≤|S|−12for every odd-cardinality ​S⊆V⁡(K).z_{v}\leq 1\quad\text{for every }v,\qquad z(E_{K}(S))\leq\frac{|S|-1}{2}\quad\text{for every odd-cardinality }S\subseteq V(K).

In particular, these inequalities imply μ⁡(K)≥|z|\mu(K)\geq|z|.

The following consequence charges the rounding loss to the sum of squared edge weights.

Lemma 4.3 (Rounding with a quadratic loss).

For every fractional matching yy in a finite simple graph KK,

μ⁡(K)≥|y|−∑eye2.\mu(K)\geq|y|-\sum_{e}y_{e}^{2}.
Proof.

Set ze=ye​(1−ye)z_{e}=y_{e}(1-y_{e}). Since 0≤ye≤10\leq y_{e}\leq 1, the vector zz is nonnegative and satisfies all vertex constraints. For an odd set SS of size s≥3s\geq 3, put m=y⁡(EK​(S))≤s/2m=y(E_{K}(S))\leq s/2. There are at most s⁡(s−1)/2s(s-1)/2 edges within SS, so Cauchy–Schwarz gives

z⁡(EK​(S))=m−∑e∈EK​(S)ye2≤m−2​m2s⁡(s−1).z(E_{K}(S))=m-\sum_{e\in E_{K}(S)}y_{e}^{2}\leq m-\frac{2m^{2}}{s(s-1)}.

The expression on the right is nondecreasing on 0≤m≤s/20\leq m\leq s/2. Consequently,

z⁡(EK​(S))≤s2−s2​(s−1)=s−12−12​(s−1)≤s−12.z(E_{K}(S))\leq\frac{s}{2}-\frac{s}{2(s-1)}=\frac{s-1}{2}-\frac{1}{2(s-1)}\leq\frac{s-1}{2}.

Singleton sets have no internal edges. Thus zz satisfies every constraint of Theorem 2, which gives μ⁡(K)≥|z|=|y|−∑eye2\mu(K)\geq|z|=|y|-\sum_{e}y_{e}^{2}. ∎

Lemma 4.4 (Repairing vertex loads).

For any nonnegative edge vector xx, put yu​v=xu​v/max⁡{1,xu,xv}y_{uv}=x_{uv}/\max\{1,x_{u},x_{v}\}. Then yy is a fractional matching on the same support and

|x|−|y|≤∑v(xv−1)+.|x|-|y|\leq\sum_{v}(x_{v}-1)_{+}.

An edge of weight one whose endpoints both have load one retains weight one.

Proof.

For every vertex vv, each incident denominator is at least max⁡{1,xv}\max\{1,x_{v}\}, so yv≤1y_{v}\leq 1. Assign each reduction xe−yex_{e}-y_{e} to an endpoint with larger load. A vertex with load at most one receives no positive reduction. A vertex with load xv>1x_{v}>1 receives at most ∑e∋vxe​(1−1/xv)=xv−1\sum_{e\ni v}x_{e}(1-1/x_{v})=x_{v}-1. Summing these bounds proves the loss inequality. The last assertion follows directly from the denominator. ∎

Proof.

Write

qe:=ℙ[e∈𝖬𝖬(Gp)],qv:=∑e∋vqe≤1,Q:=∑eqe=Eμ(Gp).q_{e}:=\mathbb{P}[e\in\MM(G_{p})],\qquad q_{v}:=\sum_{e\ni v}q_{e}\leq 1,\qquad Q:=\sum_{e}q_{e}=\E\mu(G_{p}).

γ:=1−δ,τ:=p​δ4,R:=⌈log⁡(1/δ)τ⌉.\gamma:=1-\delta,\qquad\tau:=p\delta^{4},\qquad R:=\left\lceil\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{\tau}\right\rceil. (15)

Note that we never assume UuU_{u} and UwU_{w} are independent. Their dependence is precisely what the covariance term captures.

Summing over vertices.

Combining the individual-variance and pairwise-covariance bounds, rearranging the sums, and adding the nonnegative terms with u=wu=w, we obtain

∑vVar⁡(Zv)≤τ+1/Rp​∑uruau+∑u,w|Cov⁡(Uu,Uw)|​∑vqv​u​qv​wau​aw.\sum_{v}\Var(Z_{v})\leq\frac{\tau+1/R}{p}\sum_{u}\frac{r_{u}}{a_{u}}+\sum_{u,w}|\Cov(U_{u},U_{w})|\sum_{v}\frac{q_{vu}q_{vw}}{a_{u}a_{w}}.

∑vqv​u​qv​wau​aw≤τau​∑vqv​waw=τau​rwaw≤τγ​δ,\sum_{v}\frac{q_{vu}q_{vw}}{a_{u}a_{w}}\leq\frac{\tau}{a_{u}}\sum_{v}\frac{q_{vw}}{a_{w}}=\frac{\tau}{a_{u}}\frac{r_{w}}{a_{w}}\leq\frac{\tau}{\gamma\delta},

using qv​u≤τq_{vu}\leq\tau, au≥δa_{u}\geq\delta, and aw≥γ​rwa_{w}\geq\gamma r_{w}.

Controlling the vertex loads.

Recall that xv=∑e∋vxex_{v}=\sum_{e\ni v}x_{e} is the total fractional weight assigned to edges incident to vv. We first show that the expected total overload ∑vE⁡(xv−1)+\sum_{v}\E(x_{v}-1)_{+} is small.

Consider a vertex vv covered by MCM_{C}. Since MCM_{C} is a matching, at most one crucial edge incident to vv receives positive weight, and that weight is one. Moreover, every noncrucial edge incident to vv has weight zero, since Uv=0U_{v}=0. Thus xv≤1x_{v}\leq 1, so such a vertex has no overload.

Now consider a vertex vv not covered by MCM_{C}. In this case, Uv=1U_{v}=1 and no crucial edge incident to vv receives positive weight. Therefore,

Finally, note that every edge in MC∩HM_{C}\cap H has weight one in xx. Its two endpoints have total load exactly one, since no other crucial edge can be incident to them and all their noncrucial edges have weight zero. Rounding.

We have shown that yy is a fractional matching with E⁡|y|≥(1−O⁡(δ))​Q\E|y|\geq(1-O(\delta))Q. Our final step is to show that the support of yy contains an integral matching of almost the same size.

Recall from Lemma 4.3 that for any fractional matching zz in a simple graph KK,

μ⁡(K)≥|z|−∑eze2.\mu(K)\geq|z|-\sum_{e}z_{e}^{2}.

Thus, it suffices to show that the sum of squared weights of the noncrucial edges is small.

≤2​τ​qu​vp​au2​av2​E⁡[Uu​Uv]\displaystyle\leq\frac{2\tau q_{uv}}{pa_{u}^{2}a_{v}^{2}}\E[U_{u}U_{v}] (Since E⁡fuv2≤2​τ​quv\E f_{uv}^{2}\leq 2\tau q_{uv} and γ≤1\gamma\leq 1)
=2​τ​qu​vp​au2​av2​(au​av+Cov⁡(Uu,Uv))\displaystyle=\frac{2\tau q_{uv}}{pa_{u}^{2}a_{v}^{2}}\left(a_{u}a_{v}+\Cov(U_{u},U_{v})\right)

where the first equality follows from τ=p​δ4\tau=p\delta^{4} by (15) and the second equality follows from Γ=O⁡(Q)\Gamma=O(Q) by (16). We can now apply Lemma 4.3. Recall that the positive crucial entries of yy are exactly the edges of MC∩HM_{C}\cap H, each with weight one. Consequently,

μ⁡(H∩Gp)≥|MC∩H|+|MN|≥|MC∩H|+|yN|−∑e∈Nye2=|y|−∑e∈Nye2.\displaystyle\mu(H\cap G_{p})\geq|M_{C}\cap H|+|M_{N}|\geq|M_{C}\cap H|+|y_{N}|-\sum_{e\in N}y_{e}^{2}=|y|-\sum_{e\in N}y_{e}^{2}.

Recall that Q=E⁡μ⁡(Gp)Q=\E\mu(G_{p}). Choosing δ\delta to be a sufficiently small constant times ε\varepsilon therefore gives

EH,Gp⁡μ⁡(H∩Gp)≥(1−ε)​E⁡μ⁡(Gp).\E_{H,G_{p}}\mu(H\cap G_{p})\geq(1-\varepsilon)\E\mu(G_{p}).

Finally, by (15),

R=⌈log⁡(1/δ)p​δ4⌉=O⁡(log⁡(1/ε)p​ε4).R=\left\lceil\frac{\log(1/\delta)}{p\delta^{4}}\right\rceil=O\left(\frac{\log(1/\varepsilon)}{p\varepsilon^{4}}\right).

Since HH is the union of RR matchings, every output satisfies Δ⁡(H)≤R\Delta(H)\leq R. Moreover, averaging over the randomness of HH shows that there exists a fixed subgraph HH with the same expected approximation guarantee. This completes the proof. ∎

Appendix A A Lower Bound of Ω⁡(1/(p​ε))\Omega(1/(p\varepsilon))

In this section, we show that the dependence on 1/p1/p in Result 1 is optimal. In fact, even on bipartite graphs, every sparsifier achieving a (1−ε)(1-\varepsilon)-approximation must have maximum degree Ω⁡(1/(p​ε))\Omega(1/(p\varepsilon)).

Theorem 3.

For every p∈(0,1/2]p\in(0,1/2] and sufficiently small ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exists a bipartite graph GG such that every subgraph H⊆GH\subseteq G satisfying E⁡μ⁡(H∩Gp)≥(1−ε)​E⁡μ⁡(Gp)\E\mu(H\cap G_{p})\geq(1-\varepsilon)\E\mu(G_{p}) must have maximum degree Δ⁡(H)=Ω⁡(1/(p​ε))\Delta(H)=\Omega(1/(p\varepsilon)). The same lower bound holds for randomized sparsifiers whose outputs obey the degree bound and are independent of the test realization.

Proof.

Fix p≤1/2p\leq 1/2 and ε≤1/16\varepsilon\leq 1/16. Let kk be the largest integer satisfying (1−p)k≥4​ε(1-p)^{k}\geq 4\varepsilon, and define a:=(1−p)ka:=(1-p)^{k}. By maximality of kk and since p≤1/2p\leq 1/2, we have 4​ε≤a<8​ε4\varepsilon\leq a<8\varepsilon.

The construction.

Consider a complete bipartite graph with mm vertices on each side, which we call the core vertices. Attach kk private leaves to each core vertex, as illustrated below. Each private leaf is adjacent only to its corresponding core vertex. Let GG denote the resulting bipartite graph.

Call a core vertex good if at least one of its private edges survives, and bad otherwise. Each core vertex is independently bad with probability (1−p)k=a(1-p)^{k}=a. Good vertices can be matched to private leaves, while bad vertices must rely on edges between core vertices. The full graph contains enough core edges to match almost all bad vertices, but a bounded-degree sparsifier may not.

The expected optimum in GpG_{p}.

Let BLB_{L} and BRB_{R} denote the sets of bad core vertices on the two sides. For every realization, there is a maximum matching that matches all good vertices to private leaves and then takes a maximum matching between the bad vertices. Indeed, replacing an edge incident to a good vertex by a surviving private edge never decreases the matching size, and an edge between two good vertices can be replaced by two private edges.

Consequently, the optimum is μ⁡(Gp)=2​m−|BL|−|BR|+μ⁡(Gp​[BL,BR])\mu(G_{p})=2m-|B_{L}|-|B_{R}|+\mu(G_{p}[B_{L},B_{R}]). Since |BL||B_{L}| and |BR||B_{R}| are independent Bin⁡(m,a)\operatorname{Bin}(m,a) random variables, their expected minimum is m​a−O⁡(m)ma-O(\sqrt{m}).

Moreover, conditioned on BL,BRB_{L},B_{R}, the edges between these sets survive independently with probability pp. For fixed pp and aa, this random bipartite graph contains a matching of expected size min⁡{|BL|,|BR|}−o⁡(m)\min\{|B_{L}|,|B_{R}|\}-o(m). Indeed, greedily match vertices on the smaller side while at least m\sqrt{m} unmatched vertices remain on the other side. Each attempt fails with probability at most (1−p)m(1-p)^{\sqrt{m}}, so the expected number of unmatched vertices is at most m+m​(1−p)m=o⁡(m)\sqrt{m}+m(1-p)^{\sqrt{m}}=o(m).

Taking expectations, we conclude that

E⁡μ⁡(Gp)=m⁡(2−a)−o⁡(m).\E\mu(G_{p})=m(2-a)-o(m). (23)

The limitation of bounded-degree sparsifiers.

Now consider any subgraph H⊆GH\subseteq G with maximum degree at most DD. We give HH all private edges for free, which can only increase its expected matching size.

Consider a core vertex vv with dv≤Dd_{v}\leq D core neighbors in HH. The probability that vv is bad is aa. Conditioned on this event, each of its dvd_{v} core neighbors independently fails to provide a usable edge with probability 1−p​a1-pa: either the neighbor is good, or the edge does not survive.

Thus, the probability that vv is bad and has no surviving edge to another bad vertex is at least a​(1−p​a)dv≥a​(1−p​a)Da(1-pa)^{d_{v}}\geq a(1-pa)^{D}. Such a vertex cannot be matched, even after giving HH all private edges for free. Therefore, the expected number of isolated bad core vertices is at least 2​m​a​(1−p​a)D2ma(1-pa)^{D}. Since every matching edge between bad vertices covers two such vertices, we obtain

E⁡μ⁡(H∩Gp)≤m⁡(2−a−a​(1−pa)D).\E\mu(H\cap G_{p})\leq m\left(2-a-a(1-pa)^{D}\right). (24)

Concluding the lower bound.

Suppose HH achieves a (1−ε)(1-\varepsilon)-approximation. Combining (23) and (24), and letting m→∞m\to\infty, gives a​(1−p​a)D≤ε⁡(2−a)≤2​εa(1-pa)^{D}\leq\varepsilon(2-a)\leq 2\varepsilon. Since a≥4​εa\geq 4\varepsilon, this implies (1−p​a)D≤1/2(1-pa)^{D}\leq 1/2, and therefore D≥log⁡2/(−log⁡(1−p​a))D\geq\log 2/(-\log(1-pa)).

Finally, since p​a≤1/4pa\leq 1/4, we have −log⁡(1−p​a)≤2​p​a≤16​p​ε-\log(1-pa)\leq 2pa\leq 16p\varepsilon. Consequently,

D≥log⁡216​p​ε=Ω⁡(1p​ε).D\geq\frac{\log 2}{16p\varepsilon}=\Omega\left(\frac{1}{p\varepsilon}\right).

The argument also applies to randomized sparsifiers: condition on any output HH, apply (24), and then average over the randomness of HH. ∎

Appendix B Improving the Polynomial Degree Bound

In this section, we briefly explain how the bound of Result 1 can be improved to Δ⁡(H)=O⁡(1p​ε2+1ε3).\Delta(H)=O\left(\frac{1}{p\varepsilon^{2}}+\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{3}}\right). The improvement uses the same covariance lemma, but requires a slightly different sparsification algorithm and a more refined analysis.

A modified sparsification algorithm.

Recall that qe=Pr[e∈𝖬𝖬(Gp)]q_{e}=\Pr[e\in\MM(G_{p})]. Set t=ε/2t=\varepsilon/2, and let

γ:=1−t,σ:=t21024,κ:=p​t21024,τ:=min⁡{σ​t,κ}.\gamma:=1-t,\qquad\sigma:=\frac{t^{2}}{1024},\qquad\kappa:=\frac{pt^{2}}{1024},\qquad\tau:=\min\{\sigma t,\kappa\}.

As before, let C={e:qe≥τ}C=\{e:q_{e}\geq\tau\} and N=E∖CN=E\setminus C.

Unlike sample and union, we include all crucial edges directly in HH. Since ∑e∋vqe≤1\sum_{e\ni v}q_{e}\leq 1, this contributes degree at most 1/τ1/\tau.

For noncrucial edges, we use dependent rounding [GKPS06]. More precisely, we round the fractional values be=qe/κ<1b_{e}=q_{e}/\kappa<1 to indicators JeJ_{e} with E⁡Je=be\E J_{e}=b_{e}, ensuring that the selected noncrucial degree at each vertex is at most 1/κ+21/\kappa+2. For general graphs, this can be achieved by orienting the edges arbitrarily and applying bipartite dependent rounding to the two-copy graph. The rounding also ensures nonpositive pairwise covariance between distinct incident edges within each of the two oriented groups. We return H=C∪{e∈N:Je=1}.H=C\cup\{e\in N:J_{e}=1\}. Thus every output satisfies

Δ⁡(H)≤1τ+1κ+2=O⁡(1p​ε2+1ε3).\Delta(H)\leq\frac{1}{\tau}+\frac{1}{\kappa}+2=O\left(\frac{1}{p\varepsilon^{2}}+\frac{1}{\varepsilon^{3}}\right).

This construction uses the exact marginals qeq_{e}; no efficient exact computation of them is claimed.

Changes to the analysis.

There are two main improvements over the proof of Result 1.

First, we use a stronger consequence of the same martingale argument behind Lemma 3.1. The auxiliary crucial matching MCM_{C} can be chosen so that, writing Uv=𝟏{v∉V(MC)}U_{v}=\mathbf{1}_{\{v\notin V(M_{C})\}}, for every family of LL-Lipschitz functions Fv:{0,1}V→ℝF_{v}:\{0,1\}^{V}\to\mathbb{R}, we have

∑v|Cov⁡(Uv,Fv​(U))|≤16​L​E⁡|MC|.\sum_{v}|\Cov(U_{v},F_{v}(U))|\leq 16L\,\E|M_{C}|. (25)

This follows by the same independent-block exposure argument: resampling one block changes UU in at most two coordinates, and therefore changes each FvF_{v} by at most 2​L2L. Martingale orthogonality gives the bound, which is preserved when passing to the limiting matching distribution with exact marginals.

Second, rather than bounding the overload of every vertex using the uniform slack av≥ta_{v}\geq t, we separate vertices with qv<1/2q_{v}<1/2 from those with qv≥1/2q_{v}\geq 1/2. The former have constant slack, while there are only O⁡(Q)O(Q) vertices of the latter type. Together with (25), this allows us to control the total repair loss using a total variance bound of order O⁡(t2​Q)O(t^{2}Q), instead of O⁡(t3​Q)O(t^{3}Q).

More concretely, define the noncrucial fractional frequencies by fe=κ​Jef_{e}=\kappa J_{e} and use the same fractional assignment as in the main proof, with all crucial edges available. The dependent-rounding properties give

E⁡fe=qe,E⁡fe2=κ​qe.\E f_{e}=q_{e},\qquad\E f_{e}^{2}=\kappa q_{e}.

Writing ZvZ_{v} for the corresponding auxiliary loads, the refined variance calculation gives

∑vVar⁡(Zv)≤η∗​Q,η∗:=6​κp+16​σ=O⁡(t2).\sum_{v}\Var(Z_{v})\leq\eta_{*}Q,\qquad\eta_{*}:=\frac{6\kappa}{p}+16\sigma=O(t^{2}).

Using (25) during repair, and then applying the same quadratic-rounding lemma, the resulting relative loss is bounded by

t+32​σt+2​η∗+η∗2+κp​t+16​κ​σp​t3.t+\frac{32\sigma}{t}+2\sqrt{\eta_{*}}+\frac{\eta_{*}}{2}+\frac{\kappa}{pt}+\frac{16\kappa\sigma}{pt^{3}}.

With the parameter choices above, this is less than ε\varepsilon.

This proves the improved approximation. The essential difference is that the stronger covariance estimate and refined overload analysis permit a larger noncrucial threshold, while dependent rounding removes the log factor needed by sample and union to retain crucial edges. ∎
